Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
ruminate about how event could have been prevented
I try to push them out of my mind

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'specific body parts associated with the event' is hard to reconcile clinically unless the disaster involved gruesome injury exposure, which is not supported elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items (darkness, smoke) fit disaster-related danger cues; this one points toward a different trauma context and is not coherent with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: 'Threat from strangers approaching me' implies an interpersonal danger schema. In a natural-disaster case, this is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on non-interpersonal threat cues (darkness, smoke, physical reactivity, flashback-type reliving). There are no appraisals or memory items supporting a generalized interpersonal threat pattern, so this item is a poor fit with the trauma type and overall formulation.

For a natural-disaster trauma, smoke/fire/flames can be plausible only in certain disaster contexts, but pairing them with darkness as the third trigger makes the trigger set look more like a fire-related trauma profile than a coherent general natural-disaster profile. Darkness is not impossible, but alongside smoke and flames it weakens trauma-type coherence and the trigger pattern is hard to explain without a more specific fire disaster context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
issues.explanation: Within maladaptive strategies, self-blame rumination and prevention rumination fit a perseverative threat-focused coping style, but 'I force myself to think only positive thoughts' points toward deliberate suppression/overcontrol in a different direction. It is not impossible, but in this sparse profile it sits awkwardly with the otherwise repetitive self-blaming/what-if style and is less clearly aligned with the strong Triggers ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop than another avoidance or safety strategy would be.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The profile includes only Triggers, Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies, which is acceptable given the formulation, but within Threat the selected items mix reminder-triggered reactivity with a dissociative re-experiencing item ('flashbacks'). For this trauma type and the rest of the profile, flashbacks are possible but are not well supported by the accompanying Trigger and Strategy items, which emphasize smoke/fire/weather reminders and rumination/suppression rather than dissociative reliving.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: The trigger set is coherent for a natural disaster if the event involved wildfire or smoke, but the profile does not otherwise specify a fire-related disaster context. Smoke and fire/flames are narrower and more specific than 'natural disaster' alone, so without matching memory or appraisal content they make the trigger pattern feel overly specific relative to the rest of the report.

issues.item: Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
issues.explanation: The strongest formulation links are Triggers ↔ Threat and Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, which are partly reflected by reminder-linked physical reactivity and suppression. However, the maladaptive strategies are dominated by self-blame/prevention rumination, while there are no Negative Appraisal items and no clear cross-node support for guilt/responsibility themes. This makes the rumination content weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
The fire had come without warning, a wall of flame that swept through the canyon where Carlos and his wife, Elena, had lived for forty years. He remembered the roar, the way the sky turned the color of a bruise, and the acrid, chemical smell of burning chaparral that filled the cab of his truck as they fled. That smell had lodged itself somewhere deep in his sinuses, and now, years later, it would ambush him without reason. A neighbor’s barbecue, a car backfiring, the dry, hot stillness of an August afternoon—any of it could send him back to that moment, his hands gripping the steering wheel, Elena’s voice tight with fear beside him. At seventy-five, Carlos was a retired QA engineer, a man who had spent his career finding flaws in systems. But the system that had failed him was the world itself, and he could no longer trust it.

The triggers came first, unbidden. A whiff of woodsmoke from a fireplace in December and his chest would tighten, his heart hammering against his ribs as if it were trying to escape. He would feel the heat on his skin, hear the crackling, and his hands would begin to tremble. These physical reactions—the sweating, the racing pulse—were so immediate and overwhelming that they felt like the fire itself was starting again, right there in his living room. He became hypervigilant, scanning the horizon for smoke whenever he drove, checking the stove three times before leaving the house, starting at the sound of a siren. A car door slamming too hard would make him jump, his whole body flinching as if he were bracing for an explosion. The world had become a landscape of hidden threats, and his body was always ready for the next one.

To manage this constant state of alarm, Carlos had developed a set of rigid mental routines. He would replay the day of the fire in his head, scrutinizing every decision. We should have left an hour earlier. I should have checked the evacuation routes the night before. I waited too long to fill the gas tank. This self-blame rumination was a loop he could not escape, a way of trying to impose order on chaos by finding fault in himself. He also tried to push the memories away, clenching his jaw and forcing his mind to go blank whenever an image of the flames surfaced. But these efforts only made the triggers more potent. The more he tried not to think about the fire, the more the smell of smoke seemed to find him. The more he dwelled on his mistakes, the more watchful he became, scanning for the next sign of danger. His hypervigilance fed his rumination—What else have I missed?—and his rumination made him more alert, more primed to notice any cue that might signal disaster.

This cycle grew tighter over the months and years. He stopped going for walks in the neighborhood after a neighbor’s leaf-burning sent him into a panic. He no longer visited his son’s house in the foothills, where the dry grass and tall pines felt like a tinderbox. He began to check the weather obsessively, and when the Santa Ana winds picked up in the fall, his anxiety would spike so high that he could not sleep. He would sit in the dark living room, listening to the wind, his mind churning through worst-case scenarios. Elena tried to reassure him, but he could not explain that the threat felt real, immediate, and inescapable. The physical reactivity he experienced at the smell of smoke made him certain that another fire was imminent, and that certainty drove him deeper into his mental rituals. He ruminated about how he could have prevented the first fire, and in doing so, he kept the fear alive, his body primed for a disaster that never came but always felt just around the corner.

What finally brought Carlos to seek help was a small thing: a neighbor’s trash fire, contained in a metal barrel, that sent him into a full-blown panic attack. He had locked himself in the bathroom, shaking and sobbing, while Elena called the fire department. He was ashamed, and that shame became another voice in the loop of self-blame. He was tired of being afraid, tired of the way his life had shrunk to the size of his living room. He came to the clinic hoping for a way out, but he was also terrified that the therapist would tell him the only way to get better was to face the fire again. He did not know if he could.
